name: Strelazine
description: Strelazine is the classified military-grade reflex acceleration compound that Synaptrel was designed to approximate. Where Synaptrel overclocks the peripheral nervous system broadly, Strelazine targets the cerebellum and basal ganglia with surgical precision using SNT-integrated delivery, producing reflex improvements of 45-70 milliseconds while simultaneously improving balance, proprioception, and predictive motor modeling. The result is a combatant whose body begins responding to threats before the conscious mind has finished processing them. It is not legal for civilian use under any circumstances.
effects: Elite reflex arc acceleration (45-70ms improvement — exceeds most consumer cyberware)
Predictive motor response — body begins threat response before conscious recognition
Precise fine motor control under combat stress
Integration with SNT augments for compounded enhancement
Sustained performance without the tremor risk of civilian equivalents
side_effects: Severe neurological withdrawal if used regularly — cessation causes weeks of motor impairment
Conflict with consumer-grade cyberware causing dangerous signal interference
Seizure risk at high doses even in healthy users
Users report disturbing experience of body acting before mind — loss of agency sensation
Long-term use restructures motor pathways — users become dependent on the drug to feel coordinated
Neural-direct delivery carries elevated infection and hardware damage risk
cultural_context: Strelazine is the ghost that haunts GLMZ's combat drug market — everyone has heard of it, almost no one has seen it, and the people who've used it either work for Lazarus's military division or are running very fast from people who want it back. When it surfaces on the black market, it commands prices that make it accessible only to top-tier operators, and its presence in a conflict signals that someone with serious military connections is involved. The neurological dependency it creates has destroyed the careers and lives of soldiers who were quietly addicted during service and cut off upon discharge.
story_hooks: A discharged soldier is in neurological crisis — her Strelazine dependency was never disclosed in her service record, and now she's losing motor function without access to the drug she legally cannot obtain.
A vial of Strelazine has appeared at a Tier 1 weapons market, impossibly cheap, with no clear provenance — someone is trying to start something, and the question is what.

A runner is hired to retrieve a Lazarus military courier; when she catches up, she realizes the courier is still moving with inhuman speed three hours after the op should have started — the Strelazine dose he took was not standard issue.
